packet.headline_seed: A new guideline links care for heart, kidney and metabolic diseases
packet.description_seed: A guideline treats heart disease, kidney disease, diabetes and obesity as connected conditions under one umbrella: CKM syndrome.

what: A new guideline links care for heart, kidney and metabolic diseases

clean_source_blocks.text: Some 90 percent of Americans have at least one risk factor for cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic – or CKM – syndrome, a term for potentially life-threatening conditions that are all connected. Now, experts at the American Heart Association say more of the country should be screened for one particular risk factor in the first-ever clinical guidelines for the syndrome. Excess body fat is a key driver for all of the conditions that make up CKM syndrome: obesity, cardiovascular disease, kidney disease and Type 2 diabetes, all of which are responsible for the deaths of millions of Americans each year. "Heart, kidney and metabolic conditions don't occur in isolation — they are deeply connected," Dr. Chiadi Ndumele, director of obesity and cardiometabolic research at Johns Hopkins School of Medicine, explained in a statement.

Cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic (CKM) syndrome, a serious disorder stemming from various diseases, including obesity, diabetes, chronic kidney disease, and cardiovascular disease, highlights the connections between heart, kidney, and metabolic health. Conditions related to CKM share a lot of common risk factors with cancer, but, until recently, a direct link between the two diseases has remained unclear. A new report published in the journal Circulation: Population Health and Outcomes has clarified the relationship between CKM and cancer risk through a large-scale study with over three years of follow-up.

Risk posed from excess fat should be measured by both a person's waist circumference and body mass index, the standard way obesity is diagnosed, the guidance says. While obesity screening starts at age 6, screenings for other CKM syndrome conditions typically don't happen until later in life. Screenings for heart disease typically start at age 20 for basic risk factors, but more intensive checks don't begin until around age 40-45, the association notes. Screening for Type 2 diabetes is recommended at age 35, while for kidney disease screening is recommended for older adults over the age of 60. Previous research has found that earlier screening for kidney disease – starting as soon as age 35 – would save lives.

"This guideline calls for earlier screening and care, focusing on prevention and coordinated action to reduce the risk of cardiovascular disease before serious complications develop or a major cardiac event occurs," he said. Excess weight can lead to harmful inflammation that contributes to the development of chronic disease, like cancer and heart disease. That's why maintaining a healthy weight is crucial, the association notes, to reduce the risk of CKM syndrome. Dr. Ambar Kulshreshtha, an associate professor at the Emory School of Medicine, likened the problems caused by obesity to rust. "The rust can damage the pipes, which is like your vascular system," he said. "It can damage the pump, which is like your heart. And it can damage the filters, like your kidneys."

[Lähde: Labroots]
Cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic (CKM) syndrome, a serious disorder stemming from various diseases, including obesity, diabetes, chronic kidney disease, and cardiovascular disease, highlights the connections between heart, kidney, and metabolic health.  Conditions related to CKM share a lot of common risk factors with cancer, but, until recently, a direct link between the two diseases has remained unclear.

A new report published in the journal Circulation: Population Health and Outcomes has clarified the relationship between CKM and cancer risk through a large-scale study with over three years of follow-up.

The retrospective study utilized insurance claim data from the Japanese database DeSC to identify individuals who had a checkup between April 2014 and August 2023.  The researchers found 390,901 participants without a prior cancer diagnosis and sufficient health data to analyze.  The study assigned a baseline CKM stage for each participant based on the 2023 American Heart Association guidelines, which account for cardiometabolic risk, chronic kidney disease, and atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease.  The researchers also extracted characteristics related to demographic, clinical, and lifestyle factors for each participant.

The analysis showed that individuals with a higher CKM stage had an elevated cancer risk compared to those without CKM.  The increased risk remained under 5% for stage 1 and stage 2 CKM.  However, stage 3 and stage 4 CKM conferred a 25% and 30% elevated cancer risk, respectively.  The researchers report that an increased association with cancer risk exists across cancer types, as well as in both males and females in all age cohorts.

These findings support incorporating additional procedures for cancer screening and education for patients with CKM syndrome diagnoses.  The study demonstrates the interconnections between metabolic, kidney, and cardiovascular health with cancer risk and should be routinely considered for cancer prevention strategies.

Sources: Circ, Circ Popul Health Outcomes, Ann Clin Epidemiol

payload.title: Uusi hoitosuositus tarkastelee sydän-, munuais- ja aineenvaihduntasairauksia yhtenä kokonaisuutena
payload.summary: American Heart Associationin ensimmäinen CKM-oireyhtymää koskeva kliininen ohje korostaa sydänsairauksien, munuaissairauksien, tyypin 2 diabeteksen ja lihavuuden yhteyttä sekä aiempaa varhaisempaa riskien seulontaa.
payload.content:
American Heart Associationin asiantuntijat ovat julkaisseet ensimmäisen kliinisen ohjeen CKM-oireyhtymästä, jossa sydän- ja verisuonitaudit, munuaissairaudet, tyypin 2 diabetes ja lihavuus nähdään toisiinsa kytkeytyvinä sairauksina. Ohjeen mukaan ylimääräinen kehon rasva on keskeinen taustatekijä, ja riskien arviointia pitäisi tehdä nykyistä aikaisemmin ja koordinoidummin.

## Yksi kehys usealle sairaudelle

CKM tulee sanoista cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic, eli sydän-, munuais- ja aineenvaihduntaterveyttä kuvaavasta kokonaisuudesta. Ajattelutavan lähtökohta on, että nämä sairaudet eivät useinkaan kehity erillään toisistaan. Lihavuus, sydän- ja verisuonitaudit, krooninen munuaissairaus ja tyypin 2 diabetes jakavat samoja riskitekijöitä ja voivat vahvistaa toistensa vaikutuksia.

Ohjeessa arvioidaan, että noin 90 prosentilla amerikkalaisista on ainakin yksi CKM-oireyhtymään liittyvä riskitekijä. Sairausryhmät ovat myös merkittäviä kuolleisuuden aiheuttajia. Johns Hopkinsin lääketieteellisessä tiedekunnassa työskentelevän Chiadi Ndumelen mukaan sydämen, munuaisten ja aineenvaihdunnan ongelmat ovat syvästi yhteydessä toisiinsa.

## Seulontaa aiemmin ja useammalla mittarilla

Uusi ohje painottaa erityisesti ylimääräisen rasvan mittaamista. Riskin arvioinnissa tulisi käyttää sekä vyötärönympärystä että painoindeksiä, joka on vakiintunut tapa diagnosoida lihavuutta. Pelkkä painoindeksi ei siis ohjeen mukaan riitä kuvaamaan riskiä parhaalla mahdollisella tavalla.

Nykyisissä käytännöissä eri sairauksien seulonnat alkavat eri ikävaiheissa. Lihavuuden seulonta alkaa jo 6 vuoden iässä. Sydänsairauksien perusriskitekijöitä tarkastellaan yleensä 20-vuotiaasta alkaen, mutta laajemmat tutkimukset alkavat tyypillisesti vasta noin 40-45 vuoden iässä. Tyypin 2 diabeteksen seulontaa suositellaan 35-vuotiaasta alkaen, kun taas munuaissairauden seulonta on suunnattu yleensä yli 60-vuotiaille. Aiemman tutkimuksen mukaan munuaissairauksien seulonnan aloittaminen jo 35-vuotiaana voisi pelastaa henkiä.

## Ehkäisy ennen vakavia komplikaatioita

Ohjeen keskeinen viesti on, että riskit pitäisi tunnistaa ennen vakavia sydäntapahtumia tai muita komplikaatioita. Ylipaino voi lisätä haitallista tulehdusta, joka liittyy kroonisten sairauksien, kuten sydänsairauksien ja syövän, kehittymiseen. CKM-oireyhtymään liittyvillä sairauksilla on myös yhteisiä riskitekijöitä syövän kanssa, ja tuore laaja seurantatutkimus on täsmentänyt CKM:n ja syöpäriskin välistä yhteyttä.

Emoryn lääketieteellisen tiedekunnan apulaisprofessori Ambar Kulshreshtha kuvasi lihavuuden aiheuttamia vaurioita ruosteen kaltaisiksi: ne voivat vahingoittaa verisuonia, sydäntä ja munuaisia. Ohjeen mukaan terveellisen painon ylläpitäminen on siksi tärkeä osa CKM-riskin vähentämistä.
summary_bullets: Uusi kliininen ohje kokoaa sydän-, munuais- ja aineenvaihduntasairaudet CKM-oireyhtymän alle.
Ohje korostaa ylimääräisen rasvan mittaamista sekä painoindeksillä että vyötärönympäryksellä.
Asiantuntijat painottavat varhaisempaa seulontaa ja ehkäisevää hoitoa ennen vakavia komplikaatioita.
payload.journalist_note: Artikkeli perustuu annettuun lähdepakettiin. Keskeiset väitteet rajattiin ohjeeseen, seulontaikiin, CKM-oireyhtymän määrittelyyn ja lähteissä mainittuihin asiantuntijakommentteihin ilman lisättyjä hoitosuosituksia.

Some 90 percent of Americans have at least one risk factor for cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic – or CKM – syndrome, a term for potentially life-threatening conditions that are all connected. Now, experts at the American Heart Association say more of the country should be screened for one particular risk factor in the first-ever clinical guidelines for the syndrome. Excess body fat is a key driver for all of the conditions that make up CKM syndrome: obesity, cardiovascular disease, kidney disease and Type 2 diabetes, all of which are responsible for the deaths of millions of Americans each year. "Heart, kidney and metabolic conditions don't occur in isolation — they are deeply connected," Dr. Chiadi Ndumele, director of obesity and cardiometabolic research at Johns Hopkins School of Medicine, explained in a statement.

Cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic (CKM) syndrome, a serious disorder stemming from various diseases, including obesity, diabetes, chronic kidney disease, and cardiovascular disease, highlights the connections between heart, kidney, and metabolic health. Conditions related to CKM share a lot of common risk factors with cancer, but, until recently, a direct link between the two diseases has remained unclear. A new report published in the journal Circulation: Population Health and Outcomes has clarified the relationship between CKM and cancer risk through a large-scale study with over three years of follow-up.

Risk posed from excess fat should be measured by both a person's waist circumference and body mass index, the standard way obesity is diagnosed, the guidance says. While obesity screening starts at age 6, screenings for other CKM syndrome conditions typically don't happen until later in life. Screenings for heart disease typically start at age 20 for basic risk factors, but more intensive checks don't begin until around age 40-45, the association notes. Screening for Type 2 diabetes is recommended at age 35, while for kidney disease screening is recommended for older adults over the age of 60. Previous research has found that earlier screening for kidney disease – starting as soon as age 35 – would save lives.

"This guideline calls for earlier screening and care, focusing on prevention and coordinated action to reduce the risk of cardiovascular disease before serious complications develop or a major cardiac event occurs," he said. Excess weight can lead to harmful inflammation that contributes to the development of chronic disease, like cancer and heart disease. That's why maintaining a healthy weight is crucial, the association notes, to reduce the risk of CKM syndrome. Dr. Ambar Kulshreshtha, an associate professor at the Emory School of Medicine, likened the problems caused by obesity to rust. "The rust can damage the pipes, which is like your vascular system," he said. "It can damage the pump, which is like your heart. And it can damage the filters, like your kidneys."
